newsitem.title: USA: Anti-clotting drugs work better if given longer.
newsitem.headline: Anti-clotting drugs work better if given longer.

text.p: Prolonged use of clot-fighting drugs by people who have had blocked veins in their lungs or legs may be more effective in cutting down on future clotting, a Swedish study has concluded.

The study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine said continued use of clot-busting drugs carries ongoing benefits to those who have had at least two episodes of clotting, known as venous thromboembolisms.
But the treatment also carries a risk of causing major bleeding. Such haemorrhages can be deadly, especially if they occur in the brain.

The conclusions were based on a study of 111 people who received six months of anti-clotting drug therapy and 116 others whose therapy continued indefinitely. After four years of following their progress, the researchers found that 2.6 percent of the patients who received the clot-stopping medicine indefinitely developed another clot, versus 20.7 percent who took the medication for six months.
The haemorrhage rate was 2.7 percent for the group that received six months of drug treatment compared with 8.6 percent for the volunteers who were on the drugs indefinitely.

Dr. Sam Schulman of Karolinska Hospital in Stockholm and colleagues estimated that if 1,000 patients were treated indefinitely four cases of venous thromboembolism would be avoided each month at a cost of two major haemorrhages a month.
The clot-fighting drugs used in the study were warfarin, sold under the brand name Coumadin by DuPont Co, and dicumarol, a similar drug not approved for use in the United States.
